fields.vakbeschrijving: Exploring the Grand Challenges is part of the Applications, Impact and Skills as well as the Earth System Data learning line, and sets the scene for the type of problems Earth, Climate and Technology students may end up working on. You will explore the grand challenges linked to relevant Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and discover the relevance of what you will learn in the programme to be able to come up with solution pathways from the perspective of Earth, Climate and Technology. The course revolves around a data-driven approach: by selecting readily available online datasets (e.g., on population, climate, energy use and production, biodiversity, economy) you will explore the grand challenges, and at the same time learn how to analyse, synthesise and present data. These skills will be built on in the course Geodata Fundamentals, where you will learn the essential ingredients of the data-to-insight workflow: problem formulation – data requirements and acquisition – processing, analysis, evaluation – interpretation and communication. Exploring the grand challenges is intertwined with a computer literacy and coding classes, in which you will learn the fundamentals of programming (incl. use of loops, functions, numpy, matplotlib, pandas) and apply exploratory data analysis to summarize and visualize the main characteristics (e.g., variability, correlation, distribution, uncertainty) of spatial and temporal data related to the grand challenges. Towards the end of the course, you will pick one challenge to study in more detail as a group project. In terms of skills, we will help you to get settled into the university environment and develop critical thinking skills. This includes aspects such as study planning, looking at problems from an engineering perspective and teamwork. The course will include classes on writing, presenting, academic standards (referencing, fraud, plagiarism, use of artificial intelligence) and ethical work practices. Through workshops and the group project, you will also develop skills such as social and personal skills, and presentation skills. Portfolio Throughout the programme, you will work on your portfolio. The objectives are to let you think about the relevance and relations between the courses, learning lines, and disciplines; and to reflect on your personal and academic development. A template of the portfolio will be provided, which includes assignments that are related to the skills training within the Applications, Impact and Skills courses.
fields.leerdoelen: After taking this course you will be able to: Select and justify Sustainable Development Goals relevant to a problem in the field of Earth, Climate and Technology Formulate applications of the technical skills of an Earth, Climate & Technology engineer in relation to achieving Sustainable Development Goals Collect, analyse, and synthesise relevant data and information relevant to grand challenges. Apply computer literacy and Python to process data and create visualizations that contribute to problem analysis. Transferable skills: Make a demonstrable contribution to planning, execution, and documentation of a project, including logbook and peer feedback. Apply correct referencing, structure, and academic integrity in all parts of a project. Apply ethical and transparent practices in all project activities. Write a clear, structured report and present results effectively to a non-technical audience. Reflect on your own learning process and development, including strengths and areas for improvement.
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: n.a.

fields.vakbeschrijving: This course is an introduction to the Principles of the Earth and Climate System from a global perspective. It presents the composition, dynamics and interaction of Earth’s spheres: geosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, biosphere and anthroposphere; with a larger emphasis on the first two. The rock, water and carbon cycles will be examined with conceptual or simple models to illustrate some of these interactions. The contemporary Earth and Climate System will be related to its (geological and preindustrial) past and to the different possible futures. The course provides a comprehensive perspective that will be used in following semesters as a framework to guide the application of technology to the monitoring, exploration, use and preservation of Earth’s resources (geothermal, wind and solar energy, minerals, safe climate, clean air, soil and water). Specific topics include the origin of the Earth, geodynamics, elements, minerals and rocks, the rock cycle, geological time scales, the coupled evolution of Earth’s subsurface, surface and atmosphere, and an introduction to the present-day atmosphere, oceans and cryosphere, and the effects of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions on the climate. Water transport over the surface and through the subsurface, rivers, lakes and oceans will be introduced (to be followed up in the following semester). The Climate System will be studied with a focus on natural and anthropogenic influences, the basics of the greenhouse gas effect and the effect of internal feedbacks, and an introduction to the models used to assess possible future climates. Atmospheric topics include the vertical structure of the atmosphere, global energy balance, basic thermodynamics, and an introduction to global circulation (winds). Ocean topics include an introduction to spatial variations in temperature and salinity, basic processes for sea-ice and the wind-driven and thermohaline circulations (currents). For the carbon cycle, the long-term and present-day budgets will be discussed, including the sources and sinks of natural and anthropogenic carbon.
fields.leerdoelen: Characterize the main processes of all spheres of the Earth and climate system (geosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, biosphere) (ILO1,2) Explain short- and long-term interactions between Earth’s spheres with a focus on the rock, water, and carbon cycles (ILO1, 8) Describe the evolution of the Earth System through the Earth history at geological to human time scales in view of the character and functioning of its main spheres (ILO4) Use simple numerical models to explain the effects of natural and human factors on the Earth and climate system (ILO1,3, 8) Identify different types of minerals and rocks and explain their origin (ILO4) Explain the causes and effects of contemporary and past climate change (ILO6) Explain how future climates projections are constructed through the use of climate models, the design of representative emission scenarios, and inputs from observational data (ILO8) In summary: ILOs1-4, 6, 8
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: Math, Physics (and Chemistry) from secondary school

fields.vakbeschrijving: This course will introduce the basic concepts of Newtonian Mechanics and Thermodynamics. Mechanics is the study of the motion of bodies under the action of physical forces. The course will focus on the conditions for static equilibrium, on the motion of particles and rigid bodies, and on the motion and deformation of continuums such as solids, fluids and gases. Thermodynamics is the study of how energy can be converted in different forms by applying heat and work. This course will examine how the macroscopic properties of continuums change under the influence of heat, work and mixing in terms of their temperature, volume and state of aggregation. The relevance of mechanics and thermodynamics is first discussed at theoretical and basic level whereafter it is applied and illustrated by analyses of many relevant mechanical and thermodynamical processes that take place in the solid earth, the oceans, the cryosphere and the atmosphere. These applications will illustrate and motivate the usefulness of mechanics and thermodynamics for Earth, Climate and Technology. In addition to the specific knowledge acquired, students will also practice how to conceptualise physical problems and solve them by making use of first principles and the fundamental physical laws of mechanics and thermodynamics.
fields.leerdoelen: Describe and quantify the mechanical state of materials. Conceptualise physical problems in mechanics and thermodynamics. Solve physical problems in mechanics and thermodynamics. E.g., calculate equilibrium conditions of systems, quantify motion and/or deformation of particles and continuums, quantify state and energy changes in gases and fluids. Translate and apply the physical principles from mechanics and thermodynamics to solve and analyse relevant processes in Earth and Climate Science.
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: none

fields.vakbeschrijving: This course consists of two parts: Part 1: Functions of multiple variables Part 2: Differential equations In Part 1, we extend the student's knowledge of calculus applied to functions depending on one variable to functions depending on two or more variables. We focus on the operations of differentiation and integration applied to such functions. In addition, the student's "mathematical toolbox" will be expanded with techniques for working with vectors, taking derivatives and performing integration. Topics in Part 1 are among others Vectors, inner product, cross product; Equations of lines and planes; Inverse trigonometric functions; Differentiation and integration techniques; Functions of multiple variables; Partial and directional derivatives; Extreme values of functions; Multiple integrals; Coordinate systems. In Part 2, we focus on differential equations. These are needed during the modeling of physical phenomena in the study of the earth and climate. We focus on solving some specific types of differential equations. Topics in Part 2 are among others Complex numbers; Direction field; First and second order differential equations; Taylor polynomials.
fields.leerdoelen: After a successful completion of this course the student should be able to: compute the dot and cross product of two vectors and use this in other computations; set up parametric and cartesian equations for lines and planes in three-dimensional space; determine the domain of a function of multiple variables and compute its partial derivatives and tangent planes; determine the gradient of a function of multiple variables, describe the gradient geometrically, use the gradient to compute tangent planes and directional derivatives and solve optimization problems; compute multiple integrals; decide whether it is beneficial to use polar, cylindrical and spherical coordinates to compute double and triple integrals and perform these computations; set up a mathematical model to describe engineering problems using differential equations (DEs); interpret a direction field; solve first order linear and separable DEs; use DEs to model vibrating springs; solve second order linear DEs with constant coefficients; approximate solutions to DEs using Taylor polynomials.
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: VWO Mathematics B

fields.vakbeschrijving: This course provides an in-depth introduction to the dynamic interactions between the Earth's subsurface, surface, and atmosphere and the role of water in these interactions. It integrates key concepts from geomorphology, hydrology, and atmospheric sciences , offering students a comprehensive understanding of the physical processes that shape landscapes, control water distribution, and influence climate and weather patterns. In the s urface section (Geomorphology), students will explore landform development, erosion, sediment transport, and the impact of tectonic activity on the Earth's surface. Attention is given to the role of glaciers, hillslopes, rivers, wind, and coastal processes in shaping natural environments. In the water section (Hydrology), we will explore the hydrological cycle at global and local scales. Students will develop a comprehensive understanding of the water and energy balance at the surface, precipitation climatology and extremes, unsaturated flow and infiltration, evaporation, groundwater, runoff generation and streamflow. Students will analyze hydrological data and apply modeling techniques to diagnose and predict the spatial and temporal characteristics of water storage and fluxes. Attention is given to the role water plays in connecting processes in the subsurface, surface and atmosphere at a range of temporal scales. In the atmospheric sciences portion, students will learn about atmospheric structure, and weather systems The course covers topics such as atmospheric turbulence, atmospheric thermodynamics, boundary layer meteorology, and clouds and convection . All this from the perspective of 1D analysis (vertical column) and modelling and where appropriate relate to the surface energy balance including water and vegetation surfaces and soils (land). Through a combination of lectures and practical exercises , students will develop analytical skills to assess environmental processes and their interconnections. By the end, students will be able to evaluate how landforms, water systems, and atmospheric dynamics interact to shape the natural world and respond to environmental changes.
fields.leerdoelen: · Perform calculations of components and processes of the Surface, water and atmosphere systems as to quantify the earth’s water and energy cycles. · Collect document and identify Earth surface, water and atmosphere system properties, features and observations to inform predictions with these data. · Gain skills to analyze Earth system processes, perform calculations, and use observations to improve predictions.
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: This course builds on the course Earth and Climate System (Semester 1), ECT in the Field (Semester 2) and Mechanics and Thermodynamics (Semester 1).

fields.vakbeschrijving: Geodata Fundamentals brings together knowledge of geophysics and remote sensing, of statistics, and of computer science to lay the foundations for the learning line Earth System Data . Through practical examples, this course will teach you the basic principles behind making informed decisions under uncertainty to manage subsurface resources, mitigate geohazards, or predict future weather and climate, among other applications. Building around the concept of the data-to-insight workflow, you will learn the essential ingredients to acquire, manage, process, analyze, and interpret Earth system data based on two main parts: In this first part ( Sensing and Statistics ), you will focus on the principles behind Earth system data acquisition and analysis. Uncertainty is inherent to studying and managing Earth systems, so you will start with an introduction to important concepts in probability and statistics. Then you will learn about Earth system data acquisition using a selection of geophysical and remote sensing techniques. In the second part ( Applied Statistics with Python ), you will focus on the practical use of statistics to start extracting meaningful insights from Earth system data using Python. Here you will learn to clean, transform, and analyze data and to build statistical models to predict properties related to Earth systems. You will work on case studies using the data you acquired yourself during the first part and data from other sources. At the end of this course, you will have gone through the entire data-to-insight workflow based on an initial selection of data acquisition and analysis techniques. In the following courses of the learning line Earth System Data , you will progressively build your knowledge towards more specialized or advanced techniques, for instance to tackle the specificity of time series and spatial data, which are ubiquitous around Earth systems.
fields.leerdoelen: After taking this course you should be able to: Identify and handle different types of Earth system data and file formats. Apply probability analysis and explain the relevance for decision-making under uncertainty. Explain the principles of selected geophysical and remote sensing methods. Acquire, process, and manage selected Earth system data. Apply descriptive statistics to summarize data and to understand dependencies. Fit, select, validate, and interpret statistical models to predict properties related to the Earth system. Design and implement a data-to-insight workflow using the programming language Python to answer a given question. Communicate data and results from a data-to-insight workflow effectively.
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: Exploring the Grand Challenges: Python and exploratory data analysis, transferable skills Calculus: Taylor series, differentiation, integration, vector calculus Linear algebra: matrix and vector operations

fields.vakbeschrijving: Chemistry for Earth Sciences will extend what you know from chemistry in high-school to what you need as an engineer in Earth, Climate & Technology. The topics that are addressed in this course are taken from aqueous chemistry, geochemistry, mineralogy, atmospheric chemistry and environmental chemistry. The content covers both equilibrium and non-equilibrium reactions in homogeneous phase systems (liquid, solids, gas), as well as reactions in heterogeneous systems containing mixtures of solids, liquids and gases. In these heterogeneous systems, reactions across interfaces are important. The course is based on a quantitative approach where the underlying mathematics are important so that students can understand and apply these concepts in a modeling framework. The content will expand the knowledge from high-school on acid-base chemistry, redox-chemistry, chemical thermodynamics, phase-diagrams, equilibrium and non-equilibrium chemistry, and the understanding of chemical compounds to the context of earth sciences.
fields.leerdoelen: LO 1 Describe element cycles in the earth system using fundamental thermodynamic and chemical principles. LO 2 Understand the role of chemistry and thermodynamics in the evolution of the earth and the impact of human activity on the earth system. LO 3 Apply laws of thermodynamics to solve chemical problems in liquids, solids and gases and across the interfaces between these phases. LO 4 Analyze chemical reaction equations (acid-base, photolytic, redox, ...) into algebraic equations that allow for quantitative analysis. Processes include both equilibrium, non-equilibrium. LO 5 Design experiments based on standard analytical methods to obtain chemical data on relevant environmental processes.
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: High School Chemistry, ECTB1131A+B, Basic Python Skills: numpy, pandas, matplotlib and seaborn

fields.vakbeschrijving: Linear Algebra is a branch of mathematics which is based on two mathematical operations: addition and (scalar) multiplication. Despite this deceptive simplicity, it has a vast variety of applications, both within and outside mathematics. This course is an introduction to several fundamental aspects of Linear Algebra, like vector calculation, solving systems of linear equations and matrix algebra, and notions like linear combinations, linear (in)dependence, linear transformations, subspaces, bases, dimension, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalisation, standard inner products, and orthogonal projections.
fields.leerdoelen: After taking this course you will be able to: solve systems of linear equations and make a priori statements about the number of solutions; perform matrix operations (addition, multiplication, inverse, determinant) and can determine the matrix of a linear transformation; determine whether a set of vectors is linearly dependent or linearly independent, and relate this to other concepts in linear algebra; determine dimension and bases of linear subspaces, in particular of the null space and column space of a matrix; find the (possibly complex) eigenspaces and eigenvalues of a given matrix; determine whether a matrix is diagonalisable or not, can diagonalise a matrix if possible and use this to analyse dynamical systems; find orthogonal decomposition of a vector with respect to a linear subspace.
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: High school mathematics. Complex numbers. Calculus.

fields.vakbeschrijving: This course integrates theory and skills obtained in other courses in a real-world field setting. You will discuss properties, processes and links between different parts of the Earth system in a field setting, based on your own observations and measurements. The course revolves around a trip along the Meuse river, between the Belgian Ardennes and the Dutch Limburg. Before the trip, you will prepare for the excursion by collecting information and analyzing data from the field area. In the field, you gain real-world experience with topics related to the subsurface, surface, water, (paleo)climate and weather, as well as with relevant measuring techniques. The field trip itself consists of two components. First, in an excursion-style field trip, you will learn to observe and measure various components of the Earth system through exercises at excursion stops. Then, in a group project, you will focus on acquiring data, e.g. river discharge, geophysical measurements, GNSS profiles and a LiDAR based DTM. After the field trip, you and your group will process, analyze, visualize and interpret this data, and present your findings to other groups in a poster session.
fields.leerdoelen: Identify Earth system processes and properties based on field observations of the Earth’s subsurface, surface, water cycle, and atmosphere. Discuss relations between the Earth’s spheres based on field observations. Collect data in the field using various techniques and sensors, following HSE practices, to gain experience in the process of data collection and its challenges. Apply your processing, analysis, visualization and interpretation skills on field data to investigate Earth system processes or properties. Effectively communicate findings in a poster presentation. Maintain a portfolio that demonstrates critical reflection on your personal and professional development.
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: Courses of the first semester, in particular ‘Earth and Climate System’ and ‘Exploring the Grand Challenges’. Participation in second semester courses, in particular ‘Surface, Water and Atmosphere’ and ‘Geodata Fundamentals’.

fields.vakbeschrijving: The subsurface is a key element of the Earth System. It contains natural resources (ores, geothermal heat, water), provides temporary and permanent storage (CO 2 , heat and cold, H 2 , and nuclear waste) and influences engineering operations conducted in, close to, or on the surface. Understanding the natural and engineered conditions of the subsurface is essential for a safe and sustainable future. The subsurface domain is challenging because it is hard to directly observe. Its behavior needs to be derived from fundamental physical and geological laws and by predictive models occurring across various spatio-temporal scales. A comprehensive understanding of the subsurface requires a multidisciplinary approach, integrating insights from Earth sciences (Principles of Earth Science learning line) and geodata science (Earth System Data learning line). Plate tectonics is the fundamental framework driving our understanding of geological structures and processes. The course kicks off by contextualizing the subsurface’s significance for society, relating topics such as geo-energy, subsurface storage, geo-resources, and how infrastructures interact with the shallow subsurface and how geo-hazards relate to tectonic settings. We then examine how tectonics influence the formation and evolution of sedimentary basins, showing the evolution from the deposition of sediments to their transformation (lithification) into rocks. In this part of the course, the students will also learn about the impact and occurrence of earthquakes and volcanism related to different tectonic settings and stages of basin evolution. They will develop conceptual geological models enhancing their ability to think in 2D, 3D and 4D, while connecting theory to real-world applications. We finish the course by introducing geological heterogeneities and their impact on the subsurface processes. Different scales and types of heterogeneity (sedimentary, structural, mechanical and chemical) will be described and related to the physical processes from which they originate. Students will discuss how heterogeneity and uncertainty are related, and how they impact our ability to safely and sustainably engineer subsurface applications. Throughout the course students will explore techniques from micro- to macro-scale for acquiring subsurface data in a range of practical exercises.
fields.leerdoelen: After taking this course, you will be able to: Understand why the Earth’s subsurface matters for society ( ILO 6, 8, 12). Analyse how a given geological context - from plate tectonics to basin scale - impacts a given subsurface engineering application ( ILO 1, 2, 6) Define the physico-chemical processes that alter sediments to rocks and form ore deposits ( ILO 1, 2, 4, 6). Contextualize in 2D, 3D and 4D, the formation and deformation of rocks at various scales ( ILO 1, 2, 4) Analyse geological heterogeneities in the subsurface ( ILO 1, 2, 4)
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: Knowledge from the previous Principles of the Earth System courses: Exploring the Grand challenges and Earth and Climate System

fields.vakbeschrijving: This course will focus on understanding how the global-scale motions of the atmosphere and ocean govern weather and climate. Students will learn about phenomena such as the jet stream in the atmosphere and the overturning circulation in the ocean, along with fundamental theory that helps explain how these features arise. The theory will introduce students to fluid dynamics affected by Earth’s rotation, and will be illustrated using laboratory experiments, observations and simulations. The concept of variability in the climate system will be introduced and connected to changes in large-scale oceanic and atmospheric flows. Linkages will be established between global climate patterns and consequences at more regional scales, including flooding and extreme heat events. The relevance of these mechanisms in regulating changes in our climate system will be elucidated.
fields.leerdoelen: Explain the fundamental principles guiding atmosphere and ocean motions at the planetary to regional scales Apply governing equations of motions to idealized problems and explain the underlying assumptions Interpret atmospheric and oceanic process and their variability from model and observational data Explain connections between atmospheric/oceanic processes and the climate system over different temporal and spatial scales
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: Earth and Climate System Surface water and atmosphere Calculus Fluid Dynamics

fields.vakbeschrijving: In the process from data to insights, as the central theme in the Earth System Data learning line, the role of this course lies in taking first steps in exploratory univariate data analysis in time and frequency domain, discovering patterns, features and artifacts, and attempting to describe characteristics of the observed phenomenon or process. In this semester, students will learn, from an engineer's perspective, to apply signal analysis and processing techniques to one-dimensional datasets. The basic theoretical concepts of Fourier Series and Fourier transform in continuous time are covered, to allow for signal decomposition in the frequency domain. An introduction is given into linear time-invariant systems, convolution and signal filtering, all from a continuous-time perspective. Then discrete time signals are addressed, elaborating on sampling and finite measurement duration, and turning the Fourier transform into the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) for practical application. In the second part of this course, noise is introduced, leading to random processes, first in continuous time, addressing auto- and cross-covariance. Elementary noise processes (such as white noise) are covered, as well as the aspect of stationarity. Then random sequences (in discrete time, i.e. time series) are elaborated upon, covering data interpolation, smoothing and filtering. Finally, students will learn how to construct appropriate, basic models for time series and explore functional relationships and stochastic dependencies. This course aims to convey the theoretical concepts, yet also offer extensive hands-on training, by means of examples, exercises and practical assignments, the latter including also numerical signal and time series analysis in Python with simulated, actual and even live data in class.
fields.leerdoelen: Students should be able to: Describe, manipulate, and analyze signals in both time and frequency domains , including operations such as scaling, shifting, convolution, and computation/interpretation of Fourier series and Fourier transforms. Explain the relationship between time‑domain and frequency‑domain representations and apply these insights to characterize linear time‑invariant (LTI) systems via impulse responses, frequency responses, and simple differential equations. Apply Fourier analysis to filtering , including ideal vs. causal filters. Interpret and anticipate real‑world effects such as sampling, aliasing, quantization and effects of finite time duration (such as leakage and spectral resolution). Compute the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) and interpret its numerical outcome . Identify time series as realizations of random processes and apply key statistical tools such as auto‑ and cross‑covariance functions and noise characterization in time and frequency domains. Perform time‑series processing , including filtering, smoothing, interpolation of missing data, and identify and estimate patterns, trends, and seasonality (e.g., via regression). Implement above concepts computationally using effective Python programming techniques.
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: ECTB1220A+B Geodata Fundamentals

fields.vakbeschrijving: Physical objects are described in a quantitative way with the aid of mathematics. In classical physics, all physical objects are geometric objects. The course “Fields and Waves” combines the physics of fields and waves with the mathematical tools required to describe these phenomena. The course enables students to develop essential understanding of the physical interpretation of mathematical formulations. The physical meaning of basic mathematical operations, gradient, divergence, and curl are discussed where they occur in physical problems relevant to ECT problems. The topics discussed are gravity and electric potential fields as examples of potential fields (elliptic equations), heat and mass transfer and fluid flow, electromagnetic diffusion (parabolic equations), acoustic, electromagnetic and elastic waves (hyperbolic equations). These fields and waves are used in the ECT domain to probe the Earth's atmosphere, surface, and subsurface with engineering applications in mind. While being able to find solutions for some specific cases is an important part of the course, the emphasis of the course is on learning how to describe the relevant physics with the corresponding mathematical tools, to understand the solution space, and to be able to give a physical interpretation of the solutions.
fields.leerdoelen: Explain the basic terms and concepts used in the context of potential fields, convection-diffusion fields, and wave fields [ILO 1]. Derive the equations that describe potential fields, convection-diffusion fields, and wave fields in homogeneous media [ILO 1]. Explain the relationship between medium properties and field quantities [ILO 2]. Identify the boundary conditions that turn a field and wave problem into a boundary-value problem and verify the validity of a collection of proposed solutions [ILO 1,3]. Solve field and wave equations in simple media and implement a simple numerical solver for a fields and waves problem [ILO 3, 4]. Physically interpret the solutions of an EC&T related field and wave problem [ILO 1,3].
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: C alculus Mechanics and Thermodynamics Linear Algebra

fields.vakbeschrijving: The course Fluid Dynamics covers the essential aspects of both fluid flow, and heat and mass transfer at an introductory level, offering you a starting point for your future careers where insight into processes in atmosphere, ocean, and solid earth are essential. First, we will look at the basic principles of fluid flow, starting with the different processes that influence flow and combining them into the conservation equations for mass and momentum. From here, we will then treat laminar flow, where attention will be paid to specific examples, including Hagen-Poiseuille flow, Couette flow and Darcy’s Law. Afterwards, non-dimensional analysis and dimensionless numbers are introduced, and the topic of turbulence is explored briefly. Subsequently, attention is focused on heat transfer and the equation for the conservation of energy is derived. Covered subjects include balances for simple heat-transfer problems and different transport mechanisms for heat transport, for example, heat conduction, convective heat transfer, and radiation. During the course, the strong link between education and recent research/realistic practice in engineering will be emphasized. This will be done by giving examples from realistic geophysical flows: hydrological, atmospheric, oceanic, and subsurface applications.
fields.leerdoelen: 1. Explain the physical processes and transport mechanisms that change mass, momentum and energy. [ILO 1, 2] 2. Explain the mathematical formulations, including their associated parameters, underlying assumptions and constitutive relations, for transport of mass, momentum and energy. [ILO 2] 3. Solve the conservation equations of mass, momentum and energy for (geo)physical applications. [ILO 3] 4. Analyse the flow, and transport of heat and mass in a given physical system. [ILO 2, 3]
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: Students are expected to have completed the courses: - Mechanics and Thermodynamics - Calculus - Linear Algebra - Exploring the Grand Challenges (for the python skills)

fields.vakbeschrijving: All Earth, Climate, and Technology processes, interventions and related challenges are embedded in society. Engineering solutions for a more sustainable society (e.g., wind turbines or batteries, water barriers) require processes that have implications for the Earth and climate system (e.g., greenhouse gasses, ecological impacts). Likewise, changing climatic conditions (e.g., rising temperatures, increasing drought frequencies and geohazards) have impacts on society (e.g., lowering urban liveability, increasing food insecurity). In this course, you will take challenges (e.g., for the energy transition, for climate mitigation) from stakeholders and explore the connectivity between proposed solutions and society. You will explore, analyse, and reflect on stakeholder requirements, societal needs, and the ethics of various choices, with the results communicated to others. First-hand interaction with stakeholders and exposure to a broad selection of case studies will give context and inform critical reflection on engineering solutions. Lectures and exercises -- centered around i) stakeholder consultation, ii) environmental impact assessment and life cycle assessment, iii) ethics, social responsibility, and data integrity, and iv) critical thinking -- will provide a new range of skills which can be applied to Earth, Climate, and Technology challenges.
fields.leerdoelen: Analyse the societal impact of engineering solutions. Evaluate the impact of solutions on the Earth and climate system. Critically reflect on the decisions in the engineering process from an ethical and moral viewpoint. Examine solutions considering the broad spectrum of stakeholder views. Explain results to a wide audience.

fields.vakbeschrijving: This course bridges the theoretical Earth System knowledge acquired in the previous Principles of Earth System courses with practical applications in subsurface engineering. It explores how Earth science principles underpin engineering activities in various parts of the subsurface, including: 1) the upper 50 meters of the subsurface relevant to geotechnical engineering, 2) the deeper subsurface, used for water and heat extraction, energy storage, and waste disposal, and 3) critical raw material extraction at any depth. The course emhasises the Earth Science aspects of these engineering applications, focusing on a) methods for characterising subsurface properties, b) the nature and implications of geoscientific uncertainties, and c) the relative importance of geoscientific aspects in the engineering application at stake. There is attention for, but less emphasis upon, the engineering aspects of the applications and the dynamic behavior related to the engineering, which are part of other courses of the BSc and, particularly, the more specialized tracks in the EC&T MSc. At this stage, the students will learn about how Earth System theory and practice is needed for engineering in the subsurface. The course is organised into three main components: Predictability of the subsurface characteristics and the related uncertainty This part builds directly on the preceding Earth Subsurface course, which introduced the character and variability of the subsurface. . This will be continued here focusing on the predictability of these heterogeneities and their related uncertainty. 2. Characterisation of Earth subsurface properties This component addresses methods for investigating and quantifying subsurface properties. Topics include geophysical and petrophysical methodologies, cores and cuttings as direct subsurface sediment and rock samples, and shallow subsurface methodologies such as Cone Penetration Tests. Last, upscaling of properties in geomodelling will be discussed. 3. Impact of Earth subsurface character on engineering applications Here, students integrate knowledge from the first two components to explore how subsurface characteristics influence subsurface engineering applications . This relates to the dynamic response, uncertainty propagation, project efficiency, and project safety. Given the broad scope of the subject, the course cannot cover all topics in equal depth. Instead, selected topics and applications are explored in detail to help students understand the complete workflow from data acquisition to engineering interpretation. Other topics are introduced through overview lectures to provide broader context. The selected case studies are aligned with examples from other BSc courses, ensuring that students gain both a comprehensive overview of the field and a foundation for specialisation in the MSc tracks. Lecture topics are complemented by hands-on practical exercises and project work to allow students to get to know the data, materials, and techniques actively. Alignment with the Data Learning Line is made to work on similar data and data analysis techniques. The course concludes with a summative written examination.
fields.leerdoelen: Identify how Principles of Earth System theoretical knowledge is used in shallow to deep subsurface engineering Explain the origin and nature of the character and scales of heterogeneities of Earth Subsurface properties and state Apply some direct and indirect characterisation methodologies of subsurface properties and states Infer how subsurface character and states, and their heterogeneity and predictability impact engineering, its projections and uncertainty
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: To participate in the course, active participation is needed in ECTB2110 Earth Subsurface course and a pass grade is needed for the Year 1 ECTB1120A Principles of Earth System course. Courses in the ‘Geodata Fundamentals’ learning line are expected prior knowledge particularly for the geophysics data analysis.

fields.vakbeschrijving: In this course, you will explore the rapidly changing Earth system as it responds to human activity over the past and current century. Building on concepts that you have learnt about the principles of the Earth system in the first year, in this course, you will focus on modern anthropogenic climate and environmental change, its mechanisms, impacts and subsequent implications for living systems. You will investigate how key components of the climate system, i.e. the atmosphere, ocean, land, carbon and biosphere interact under the influence of human-induced forcing. You will go from understanding global-scale trends to assessing their regional and local impacts, such as extreme heat and precipitation, sea-level rise, ice melt, wildfires and biodiversity loss. Along with understanding these impacts, you will also understand cross-cutting concepts such as uncertainties, tipping points, compound events and the challenge of comparing models with real-world observations, all of which are highly relevant to the discussion of the aforementioned topics. This course will have a major part which uses a hands-on approach. Through guided computational exercises using platforms like KNMI Climate Explorer and Climate Reanalyzer, you will learn to analyze climate datasets, interpret model outputs, and assess patterns in both mean and extreme events. You will develop practical skills in evaluating climate projections (from global and regional simulations) while learning the coupling of atmosphere, land, ocean and carbon systems in a warming climate. This course will emphasize understanding and application over memorization and hence, we have short, analytical assignments throughout the course with a final project that links data interpretation to contemporary climate issues. By the end, you will be equipped to critically analyze ongoing climate and environmental change shaping our planet today by bridging concepts from theory and data.
fields.leerdoelen: After taking this course, you will be able to: 1. Explain how anthropogenic climate change is modeled, monitored and analyzed 2. Describe how engineering choices lead to different SSP scenarios 3. Distinguish significant trends in global and regional climate change from internal variability 4. Identify the main sources of uncertainty of estimates in view of their complexity and characteristic spatial and temporal scales of variability 5. Discuss regional climate impacts in light of global warming 6. Describe how the living environment is impacted by changes in the natural and built environment 7. Discuss the ethical and societal impact of research and engineering solutions
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: You're expected to know basic information about Atmosphere and Ocean Dynamics as well as Signals and Time Series. You should also have experience in Python programming from previous courses.

fields.vakbeschrijving: The goal of the course is twofold. First, students will learn to work with new sensing techniques from earth observation and geophysics that extend their knowledge from Year 1. These techniques include multispectral and seismic imaging techniques. Second, after this course, students will have obtained the knowledge and skills to critically derive information from uncertain 2D Earth System data. Students will get acquainted with the concept of spatial analysis and students will be trained in acquisition, processing, and analysis of 2D Earth System data. Building on the fundamentals acquired in previous courses of the Earth System Data learning line (Grand Challenges, Geodata Fundamentals, Signals and Time Series), students will advance their skills towards notably imaging systems and two-dimensional datasets. Image acquisition systems provide spatial data that varies in terms of coverage and volume, quality, and complexity. In the Sensing and Spatial Analysis course, students will learn to work with processing techniques to estimate variable properties and the uncertainties in these estimates at a given spatial location. These processing techniques incorporate spatial variability, data uncertainty and scales in different ways and include deterministic and stochastic interpolation, 2D Fourier analysis, supervised and unsupervised classification, and spatial filtering and smoothing. Students will use the different spatial processing methods on data from known and newly introduced sensing techniques. Students will notably learn about principles and properties of multispectral remote sensing and geophysical data, while students will apply spatial analysis techniques on known sensor data such as meteorological data, GNSS, photogrammetry and laser scanning. Students will learn to use QGIS and Python as tools to work with realistic scenarios of spatial analysis using data sets consisting of thousands to millions of observations. This course is directly related to the 2nd years Fieldwork Project, that runs in the same semester. Students will process multispectral remote sensing data in the Fieldwork Project using methods introduced in this course.
fields.leerdoelen: [LO1] Explain the physical and technical principles behind spatial sensing techniques including multispectral remote sensing and geophysical techniques. [LO2] Apply spatial analysis techniques in an efficient workflow on real spatial data of various data types using a GIS system and Python. [LO3] Evaluate spatial sensor techniques against each other in terms of coverage and sampling schemes, effort required, and quality. [LO4] Apply different mathematical and statistical techniques to assess spatial continuity, variability and scales. [LO5] Estimate uncertainty of spatial measurements and derived parameters. [LO6] Differentiate between different spatial analysis methods of interpolation, classification, smoothing and filtering in terms of computational efficiency, robustness, ease of use and quality of results.
fields.toelatingseisen_nld: There are no formal admission requirements
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: Theory and skills from Calculus, Linear Algebra, Geodata Fundamentals, Signals and Time Series and Field and waves Basic programming skills in Python (from Grand Challenges)

fields.vakbeschrijving: This course introduces students to the essential mathematical "building blocks" and techniques required to solve systems of equations, which play an important role in many practical applications across the earth sciences. We will introduce the numerical methods used for modelling natural earth system phenomena (e.g. ground water flow, ocean circulation and atmospheric flow) and induced responses (e.g. seismic wave propagation). The students will work on simplified simulation approaches for the governing equations underlying these subjects. These governing equations will represent the many processes that are at play in the Earth systems. We will first connect the governing equations in the context of different applications in earth sciences and explain the principles of discretization in time and space. Students will learn how different choices in discretization in space and time influence the accuracy and reliability of numerical results. Beyond applying numerical methods, students will design workflows that move from describing an earth system process, to formulating the governing equations, and finally to implementing and interpreting numerical simulations. This will help them relate their simulation outcomes back to the original scientific problems. Foreseen topics included in the course are: overview of different systems of coupled equations and fields of application the “Why” from continuous world to discrete representation numerical integration numerical interpolation discretization methods for partial differential equations (1D, 2D..) application to diffusion, advection, wave and/or Laplace equations, potential fields numerical optimization high performance computing
fields.leerdoelen: After completion of this course, students will be able to: explain the relevance and provide examples of numerical modelling across different spheres of our Earth system. apply numerical discretization, integration and optimization techniques to solve systems of differential equations. assess how different error sources in numerical solutions arise from discretization and integration choices. design a workflow from natural earth system phenomena via governing equations to numerical implementation and simulation
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: Mathematical foundations Prior courses in calculus and linear algebra provide the mathematical tools required to understand and manipulate governing equations, including analytical solution methods and vector- and matrix-based formulations. Physical and governing equations Courses covering fields and waves and fluid dynamics introduce fundamental physical principles and conservation laws that underpin the equations and models used in this course. Computational and data skills Previous experience with programming and geospatial data analysis equips students with the skills needed to implement models numerically, process datasets, and analyse results in practical sessions ( geodata fundamentals and exploring the grand challenges ).

fields.vakbeschrijving: Central to this course is data collection in the French regional parc of the ‘Baronnies Provençales’ (in the Drôme Region). In teams of three, you will prepare, execute, and report on an Application-Driven Project based on a Field Survey. In short, you are given a ~50km 2 area in the southeast of France for you and your team to do fieldwork so that you collect – bottom to top – scientific data to solve a scientific and/or engineering problem. Before the field work, there will be two weeks of preparation in Delft. During these weeks, your time will be dedicated to equipping you with solid field-based workflows to characterise the geosphere (geology), the atmosphere (atmosphere observations) and everything in between (hydrosphere and biosphere; Remote sensing). In the second preparation week, you will also get training for a specific Application-Driven Project (ADP). The outcome of this second preparation week is the plan of your field campaign that combines field-based technologies, methods, and workflows. During field work (weeks 4.6, 4.7, and 4.8), you start with general field activities, which we call the ‘Field Survey’ and aim at having you characterising the Earth’s spheres with a focus on the geosphere. You do that by following the scientific method. In all phases of your field work, you will be acquiring Earth and Climate data daily, in a systematic manner. There, for about one third of your time, you will be conducting specific field activities for your ADP. The “FIELD survey” from your area will feed data to your selected “application-driven PROJECT”, together making your FIELD PROJECT unique. With additional field methods and technologies, you will be able to work on a real problem with your data. Once you are back to Delft and for two weeks, you will report on your team’s findings about your area and ADP in an oral presentation. Students with disabilities who cannot participate in the field work would join a team and assist them either from Delft or the field camp. Field Project = Field Survey + Application-Driven Project (ADP)
fields.leerdoelen: After taking this course, you will be able to: Design a manageable field survey plan that combines field-based technologies, methods, and workflows aimed at solving an application-driven project. ILO5, ILO10 Execute field-based workflows to efficiently and systematically acquire Earth and Climate data in the field in a quality-controlled manner to characterize the Earth’s spheres and their interactions, while following scientific, health, safety, and environmental standards. ILO4, ILO5, ILO10, ILO11 Interpret Earth and Climate data acquired by you, your team, and neighboring teams you share areas with, as an interconnected puzzle of the Earth’s spheres. ILO2, ILO4, ILO10, ILO13 Construct deliverables (e.g., time series, maps, cross-sections, logs, etc...) that characterize, quantify, and visualize Earth’s spheres using Earth and Climate field data as well as open-access data. ILO2, ILO10, ILO11 Evaluate the quality of the deliverables constructed with data from a field study area using suitable methods, metrics, and validation data, and discuss quality, sources of error, and uncertainties associated with field measurements. ILO10, ILO11, ILO13 Reflect critically and independently on the interpretation of your field data and results and that of other teams, to inform and adjust your team’s decisions, in all phases of a field project. ILO13 Manage a Field Project with your team from its initiation to its conclusion, through constructive peer feedback and appropriate presentation techniques. ILO5, ILO10, ILO11
fields.toelatingseisen_nld: Prerequisites courses in the EC&T program: Earth and Climate System (Y1S1); Surface, Water and Atmosphere (Y1S2); Earth’s Subsurface (Y2S1); Sensing and Spatial Analysis (Y2S2). Recommended knowledge from courses in the EC&T program: EC&T in the Field (Y1S2); Signal and Time Series (Y2S1); Atmosphere and Ocean Dynamics (Y1S1); Climate and Environmental Change (Y2S2); Geology for Engineering (Y2S2).
fields.cr_expected_prior_knowledge_nld: What you need: Writing, Discipline, Computer Literacy, and Reading comprehension What you will gain: Independence, Critical thinking, Teamwork, Project and Time management
